source.title: VC Theoretical Explanation of Double Descent

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper empirically models double-descent behavior using VC bounds and weight-norm estimates, rather than reproducing the original studies’ methods.
record.gate_note: The paper cites other work on sample-wise nonmonotonicity, but those cited results are not recorded as this study’s results. Its own sample-size sweep is included as figure-only evidence. It does not report complete epoch-wise double-descent curves for its multilayer networks.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own empirical test-error curves for random-feature SVM and LS classifiers over feature count, noise and sample count. It also reports curves for SGD-trained networks restricted to the second-descent region, and fits them with VC bounds. This is a different method aimed at the same question. It also argues that second descent reflects falling VC-dimension (norm of weights), which bears on V7.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also claim that classical VC bounds fully explain double descent. In their account, first descent is error minimization at growing VC-dimension, and second descent is norm minimization at zero training error with falling VC-dimension. They add that second descent beats first descent mainly for large, clean, well-separable data, and that with label noise it can be worse.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses VC-bound modeling and weight-norm-based VC-dimension estimates with random-feature classifiers and restricted multilayer-network experiments, rather than reproducing the original studies’ empirical procedures.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curves and interpolation thresholds vary with classifier (SVM versus LS), feature map (ReLU versus RFF), label noise, training sample count, architecture, width, and epoch setting. The paper also reports dependence of the VC-bound fit on the constants a1 and a2.

fits_no_version.finding: The interpolation threshold depends on the learner: for SVM it is set by the number of support vectors and rises with label noise; for LS it stays at ≈n=800 regardless of noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The peak location is set by a learner-specific complexity count (support vectors vs sample size), not by raw parameter count alone.

record.peer_reviewed: Under review as a conference paper at ICLR 2023
record.problems: Many outcomes are presented only in figures; the multilayer-network epoch sweeps are restricted to the second-descent region. The proposed VC-dimension estimates for general multilayer networks are hypotheses for restricted settings, and the authors note that analytic estimates for general DL networks are not available.
record.rows_left_out: No additional qualifying results omitted. Figures 5–11 and 13–16 provide further VC-bound modeling results, but the accompanying text does not state separate test-error outcomes for each plotted dataset, architecture, or setting; their plotted values are not available in the supplied text.

untested.parts: The full fall-rise-fall curve in deep networks; the multilayer experiments cover only the second-descent region by design.
The whole epoch-wise curve; the epoch sweeps (Fig 4b, 13b, 14b, 16b) are shown only where training error is under 1%, and the text does not describe the test-error shape.
A single complexity measure predicting peak location across size, epochs and samples is not tested.
Multiple or triple peaks, and removal of the peak by optimally tuned regularization (SVM C fixed at 64).
Deep networks; only fixed-size random-feature LS classifiers were tested.

missing.what: Norm-squared of weights and estimated VC-dimension versus N: rising, then decreasing past the threshold and closely following the shape of second-descent test error.
With noisy labels, second-descent test error is worse than the optimal first-descent model.
N=2000 comparison: LS (linear) test error 3.7% with norm 3.3, versus SGD net 3.1% with norm 2.3.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Its random-feature setup follows Belkin et al., but it reports its own curves. Many outcomes are figure-only; the states rely on the authors' wording. The appendix datasets (Figs 8–11) and the two-layer and LeNet figures have no stated test-error outcomes. The VC-bound fit depends on the constants a1 and a2, which were chosen empirically.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test the full fall-rise-fall model-size curve in deep networks; its multilayer-network experiments focus on the second-descent region.
The multilayer-network epoch sweeps are restricted to the second-descent region; the full fall-rise-fall curve over training time is not tested.
The sample-size results are shown for fixed-size random-feature networks; the text does not give numerical test errors or describe the plotted direction in detail.
The empirical model-class coverage is limited to the classifiers and network settings studied here, not all model classes.
The paper does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
The paper studies noise effects, but does not test multiple or triple peaks, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The paper does not show that using an effective parameter count converts the second-descent curve into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.reason: Per the text (no row), with noisy labels second-descent performance is worse than the optimal first-descent model. So the second descent does not subsume the U-curve optimum there.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Section 2, Figure 3 discussion explicitly reports worse second-descent generalization relative to the optimal first-descent model with noisy labels, qualifying the claimed subsumption of the classical optimum.

relationships.reason: The text states double descent appears as a function of training-sample count, implying that larger n hurts near threshold. Values are figure-only; R14, R15.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: Appendix A, Figure 12 discussion explicitly reports double descent over training-sample count for fixed networks with N=500 and N=1500, supporting a region where additional samples worsen test error.

relationships.reason: No visible first descent on clean data; both descents appear with label noise; R5, R6.
relationships.display_finding: Clean data showed no visible first descent, while label noise produced both descents.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: Section 2, Figure 3 discussion states that clean-data SVM has no visible first descent, whereas noisy-data SVM exhibits both descents. This supports the tested noise-dependence component; multiple peaks and optimal regularization remain untested.

relationships.reason: A clear peak appears even with 0% label noise. Noise only degrades and flattens the curve, with no stated peak growth; R7, R8.
relationships.display_finding: A clear peak appeared at 0% label noise, while added noise degraded performance and flattened the curve without reported peak growth.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Section 2 reports both descents with clean and noisy labels, and flattening of second descent as noise increases. A clean-data peak does not contradict V6's alternative variance mechanism, which is untested. V6 does not require peak growth with noise; optimal regularization is also untested.

relationships.condition: Random-feature SVM/LS, VC-dimension estimated as min(||w||², N+1)
relationships.reason: Based on the text (no row): VC-dimension rises with N and then falls past the threshold. The shape of test error tracks the norm-squared, and the authors frame second descent as lower complexity.
relationships.display_finding: Estimated VC-dimension rose with N and fell beyond the threshold, while test error tracked squared weight norm, linking second descent to lower complexity.

source_check.condition: Random-feature SVM/LS, VC-dimension estimated as min(||w||², N+1)

They do not establish an effective parameter count or demonstrate that error becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve when plotted against it. The evidence is indirect for V7's exact claim.
